title: Evolution
tagline: Evidence for evolution, natural and sexual selection, drift, coevolution, speciation, phylogenies, macroevolution and human origins
summary: Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution, as Theodosius Dobzhansky put it. This course presents the evidence that life has evolved, the processes that change populations — natural and sexual selection, mutation, drift and gene flow — coevolution between species, the origin of species, how phylogenies are read and built, the large-scale patterns of the fossil record, and the evolution of our own species.
overview: Evolutionary biology explains why living things are the way they are. It asks two kinds of question: historical ones — how organisms are related, when lineages split, how the major groups and their structures arose — and mechanistic ones — which processes change populations from generation to generation, and how those processes produce adaptation, new species and the large-scale patterns of the fossil record. The answers connect every other part of biology, from the genetic code shared by all cells to the behaviour of animals and the structure of ecosystems, and they matter practically for antibiotic and pesticide resistance, crop breeding, conservation and the tracing of epidemics.

The course starts with the evidence that life has evolved, then builds the theory of how it evolves, quantitatively and at first-year level: the Hardy–Weinberg principle, selection in haploid and diploid populations, mutation, the Wright–Fisher model of drift with the fixation probabilities 1/2N and about 2s, gene flow, and the neutral theory and molecular clock. It then applies these tools to sexual selection, coevolution and speciation, turns to phylogenetics — how trees are read and built — and to macroevolution over geological time, and ends with the evolution of our own species, using fossils and ancient genomes.

Evolution is easy to state and easy to misunderstand. The common difficulties are thinking about populations rather than individuals, about probabilities rather than certainties, and about deep time; and resisting the intuitions that evolution has goals, that selection works for the good of the species, and that trees are ladders of progress. Each lesson flags these misconceptions and works through numerical examples and simulations, so that verbal arguments can be checked against what the models actually predict. The full population-genetic theory is developed later in Population and Quantitative Genetics.
outcomes: Evaluate the main lines of evidence for common descent — fossils dated radiometrically, homology, biogeography and molecular data — and explain why their agreement is decisive.
Derive the Hardy–Weinberg proportions and use them to calculate genotype frequencies and to test a sample with a χ² test.

Calculate changes in allele frequency under haploid and diploid selection, including dominance, selection against recessives and heterozygote advantage, and predict the response of a quantitative trait with the breeder's equation.

Explain genetic drift with the Wright–Fisher model and calculate fixation probabilities (1/2N for a neutral allele, about 2s for a beneficial one), the decay of heterozygosity, effective population size and the effects of gene flow.
Explain the neutral theory of molecular evolution and use a calibrated molecular clock to estimate divergence times, stating its assumptions.
Analyse sexual selection, coevolution and the evolution of the sex ratio using Bateman gradients, frequency-dependent models and Fisher's principle.

Compare species concepts, quantify reproductive isolation, and explain how isolation evolves through Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibilities, reinforcement, selection against gene flow and polyploidy.
Read phylogenetic trees correctly, count possible trees, and build trees by parsimony and distance methods with corrected distances.
Interpret macroevolutionary patterns — rates in darwins, diversification and extinction, adaptive radiation, mass extinctions and the origin of novelties — on the geological time scale.
Describe the well-established evidence on human evolution, from the hominin fossil record to ancient genomes and archaic admixture, and distinguish it from open questions.

chapters.title: Evidence for evolution
chapters.summary: Fossils, homology, biogeography and molecular evidence, and the development of evolutionary thought from Lamarck to Darwin.

chapters.title: Natural selection and adaptation
chapters.summary: Variation, heritability and differential reproduction, and what adaptation can and cannot achieve.

chapters.title: Mutation, drift and gene flow
chapters.summary: The other forces that change allele frequencies, and the neutral theory of molecular evolution in outline.

chapters.title: Sexual selection
chapters.summary: Competition for mates, mate choice and the evolution of differences between the sexes.

chapters.title: Coevolution
chapters.summary: Arms races between hosts and parasites and between predators and prey, and the coevolution of mutualists.

chapters.title: Species and speciation
chapters.summary: Species concepts, reproductive isolation, and allopatric and sympatric speciation.

chapters.title: Phylogenetics: reading the tree of life
chapters.summary: Tree thinking, homology and homoplasy, parsimony and the reconstruction of evolutionary history.

chapters.title: Macroevolution
chapters.summary: Rates of evolution, adaptive radiation, mass extinction and the origin of evolutionary novelties.

chapters.title: Human evolution
chapters.summary: The hominin fossil record, ancient DNA, and the origin and spread of modern humans.

history.title: Darwin and Wallace announce natural selection
history.detail: Papers by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached the idea independently in the Malay Archipelago, were read at the Linnean Society of London on 1 July 1858.

history.title: On the Origin of Species
history.detail: Darwin's book, published on 24 November 1859, set out the evidence for descent with modification and the mechanism of natural selection.

history.title: The mathematical theory of evolution
history.detail: Fisher's The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930), Wright's 'Evolution in Mendelian populations' (1931) and Haldane's The Causes of Evolution (1932) reconciled selection with Mendelian genetics and founded theoretical population genetics.

history.title: Genetics and the Origin of Species
history.detail: Dobzhansky's book joined population genetics to studies of natural populations of Drosophila and described isolating mechanisms and the Dobzhansky–Muller model of hybrid incompatibility.

history.title: The biological species concept
history.detail: Mayr's Systematics and the Origin of Species defined species by reproductive isolation and made the case for allopatric speciation, a pillar of the Modern Synthesis.

history.title: Phylogenetic systematics
history.detail: Hennig's Grundzüge einer Theorie der phylogenetischen Systematik (English edition 1966) made shared derived characters the basis of classification and founded cladistics.

history.title: The neutral theory of molecular evolution
history.detail: Kimura argued in Nature that most molecular substitutions are selectively neutral and fixed by drift, so that they accumulate at the mutation rate; King and Jukes made the same case in 1969.

history.title: Punctuated equilibrium
history.detail: Eldredge and Gould proposed that many fossil species show long stasis interrupted by rapid change associated with speciation, starting a long debate on tempo and mode in the fossil record.

history.title: Darwin's finches on Daphne Major
history.detail: Peter and Rosemary Grant began their annual study of Galápagos finches, later documenting natural selection on beak size during the 1977 drought and its evolutionary response.

history.title: The E. coli long-term evolution experiment
history.detail: On 24 February 1988 Richard Lenski founded twelve populations of Escherichia coli propagated by daily transfer, with a frozen record every 500 generations, which has passed tens of thousands of generations.

references.title: Evolution, 5th edition
references.authors: Douglas J. Futuyma and Mark Kirkpatrick
references.note: The standard undergraduate textbook: thorough on population genetics, speciation, phylogenetics and macroevolution, with clear figures and up-to-date examples.

references.title: Evolution
references.authors: Nicholas H. Barton, Derek E. G. Briggs, Jonathan A. Eisen, David B. Goldstein and Nipam H. Patel
references.note: Integrates molecular biology, genomics, development and palaeontology with population genetics; strong on the origin of life, the tree of life and evo-devo.

references.title: Evolution, 3rd edition
references.note: A clear, quantitative introduction with worked population-genetic models, good chapters on adaptation, species and the fossil record.

references.title: Evolution: Making Sense of Life, 3rd edition
references.authors: Carl Zimmer and Douglas J. Emlen
references.note: An accessible, richly illustrated first-year text built around case studies; good for tree thinking and human evolution.

references.title: Speciation
references.authors: Jerry A. Coyne and H. Allen Orr
references.note: The authoritative monograph on species concepts, reproductive isolation, the geography of speciation and the genetics of hybrid incompatibility.

references.title: Inferring Phylogenies
references.note: The reference on parsimony, distance, likelihood and Bayesian methods, tree counting and the bootstrap, by the developer of many of them.

references.title: Sexual Selection
references.note: The classic synthesis of theory and evidence on mate competition, mate choice and ornaments.

references.title: 40 Years of Evolution: Darwin's Finches on Daphne Major Island
references.authors: Peter R. Grant and B. Rosemary Grant
references.note: A first-hand account of natural selection, hybridisation and speciation measured in the wild over four decades.
